newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Thousands of Bosnian refugees to quit Switzerland.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of Bosnian refugees to quit Switzerland.

text.p: Thousands of Bosnian refugees faced a deadline to leave Switzerland for their war-scarred homeland on Wednesday or find a legal way to extend their stay as the prospect of forced repatriations loomed, officials said.

The deadline applied to a first wave of some 6,300 single people or childless couples still here after fleeing to Switzerland to escape ethnic warfare between Croats, Moslems and Serbs in the former Yugoslav republic.
"We are getting a lot of applications today for our return assistance progamme," said Roger Schneeberger, a spokesman for the Federal Bureau for Refugees in Berne.
"We hope as many people as possible will return voluntarily, and this is why we are offering them assistance that should make it easier for them to return and integrate in Bosnia."
Since the assistance scheme began last July, some 4,260 of the 18,000 refugees taken in have applied for Berne to pay their transport costs and a travel allowance for the return trip to Bosnia.

Once there, they can collect 800 Swiss francs ($546) in start-up aid; another 4,000 francs per adult and 2,000 francs per child for reintegration aid to build or rent homes or open businesses; and 1,000 francs per family for living expenses.
As of last Friday, 2,831 Bosnians had returned home and claimed the money, Schneeberger said. More are already there but have not yet been officially recorded.
Returnees must be in Bosnia by the end of May to collect the full amount of Swiss assistance. The amount of aid then drops by two-thirds until the end of August.
Of the 6,300 people whose deadline to return was now expiring, many have applied to cantonal authorities for permission to extend their stays, but the total was unclear.
Many were pregnant women, people undergoing medical treatment or finishing apprenticeships, or couples of mixed ethnic background who will find it hard to reintegrate.
Others will be forced to go home soon, Schneeberger said.
"We have recommended cantons exercise restraint on forced repatriations from May 1 until the end of August," he said.

Suzanne Auer, spokeswoman for the Swiss Refugee Aid charitable group in Berne, said some cantons could start forced repatriations even sooner and criticised the government for threatening force to send refugees into an uncertain future.
"Again and again we have heard people say that as soon as the situation improves, they know their lives are safe and they know how they can live, they will return," she said.
"People really want to go back. Their lives here are nothing special," she added, expressing regret that Germany and Switzerland were adopting approaches that relied on force.

She estimated 3,500 refugees had returned voluntarily, but said many who remain -- primarily Moslems -- did not want to go back now because other ethnic groups were ignoring international accords guaranteeing their right to return to their homes.

Several German states have started forced reptriations of refugees from among the 320,000 Bosnians they took in. The United Nations refugee agency has criticised Germany, saying too many deportations could destabilise the region.
Switzerland is letting some 5,300 people with recognised refugee status stay indefinitely and has granted humanitarian residence permits to another 700.
Some 1,100 deserters and conscientious objectors may remain while Berne gauges how Bosnia's amnesty law is implemented.
($ = 1.464 Swiss Francs)
